Protecting our Students in Schools Act of 2025

This bill prohibits the use of corporal punishment in schools that receive federal funding.

Specifically, the bill authorizes the Department of Education (ED) to take specified actions (e.g., withholding funds and issuing cease-and-desist orders) for schools that allow school personnel, law enforcement officers, or school security guards to subject students to corporal punishment.

The bill also establishes enforcement provisions, including a private right of action for a student who has been subjected to corporal punishment.

Each state educational agency (SEA) that receives federal funding must submit specified information to ED, including a school climate report that describes the SEA's policies and procedures related to exclusionary and aversive discipline practices in schools.

Additionally, the bill authorizes ED to award three-year grants to SEAs and, through them, subgrants to local educational agencies to implement positive behavioral interventions and supports to address student behavior and reduce exclusionary and aversive discipline practices.

ED must promulgate regulations as necessary to ensure compliance with the bill. The Department of Defense and the Department of the Interior must ensure that the schools they operate or fund also comply with these regulations.

Rural Health Training Opportunities Act

This bill modifies and expands the Health Profession Opportunity Grants (HPOG) program. Specifically, the Administration for Children and Families must prioritize grant applications for demonstration projects in rural areas, and projects must include assistance for the transportation costs of program participants. (The HPOG program provides education and training to low-income individuals for in-demand occupations in the health care field.)

This bill expands the required components of the National Health Security Strategy (a coordinated strategy among federal, state, local, and tribal entities for public health emergency preparedness and response).

Specifically, the National Health Security Strategy must address (1) coordination of federal efforts related to biological attribution (i.e., determining the source of biological hazards and pathogens of pandemic potential); and (2) early warning of emerging biological, chemical, and radiological threats, including synthetic drugs and fentanyl.

Protecting Young Minds Online Act

This bill requires the Center for Mental Health Services within the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to implement a strategy for addressing the effects of social media and other new technologies on children's mental health.

Essential Skills and Child Care for Health Professions Act

Pathways to Health Careers Act

This bill provides funding for, reauthorizes through FY2030, and makes a variety of changes to certain grants administered by the Department of Health and Human Services that provide education and training to low-income individuals for health care occupations, including by establishing a new competitive grant for projects designed to train low-income individuals in allied health professions.

", "updateDate": "2026-11-06T19:32:13Z", "versionCode": "00" }, { "actionDate": "2025-04-01", "actionDesc": "Introduced in House", "bill": { "congress": 119, "number": "2545", "originChamber": "House", "originChamberCode": "H", "title": "Financing Our Energy Future Act", "type": "HR", "updateDateIncludingText": "2026-11-06", "url": "https://api.congress.gov/v3/bill/119/hr/2545?format=json" }, "currentChamber": "House", "currentChamberCode": "H", "lastSummaryUpdateDate": "2026-11-06T19:13:10Z", "text": "

Financing Our Energy Future Act

This bill allows a publicly traded partnership to derive income from certain clean energy-related activities and still be treated as a partnership for federal income tax purposes.

As background, a publicly traded partnership is a partnership whose interests are traded on an established securities market (or readily tradable on a secondary market). A publicly traded partnership generally is treated as a corporation for federal income tax purposes unless 90% or more of such partnership’s gross income is qualifying income.

Under current law, qualifying income includes 

  • interest and dividends;
  • real property rents;
  • gain from the sale (or disposition) of real property;
  • income from certain activities related to minerals and natural resources, source carbon dioxide, and the transportation or storage of certain fuels; and
  • gain from the sale (or disposition) of a capital asset or commodities.

Under the bill, the qualifying income is expanded to include income derived from  

  • electric power (or thermal energy) generated from renewable energy sources (e.g., wind and solar energy), qualified gasification projects, or advanced nuclear facilities;
  • accepting or processing open-loop biomass or municipal solid waste (by certain facilities);
  • the storage of electric power or thermal energy using certain energy storage technology;
  • the generation, storage, or distribution of electric power (or thermal energy) using combined heat and power system property;
  • fuels that use certain carbon oxides as primary feedstock;
  • certain renewable chemicals;
  • transportation or storage of liquefied or compressed hydrogen;
  • the conversion of renewable biomass; and
  • certain carbon capture and sequestration facilities.

Americans Giving Care to Elders Act of  2026 or the AGE Act of 2026

This bill provides a new nonrefundable federal tax credit for 20% of a taxpayer’s expenses to care for an older adult, subject to limitations. The amount of expenses incurred during any year that may be taken into account for the tax credit may not exceed $6,000. Further, the tax credit begins to phase out once a taxpayer’s adjusted gross income exceeds $120,000.

The tax credit applies to expenses to care for certain relatives or members of the taxpayer's household who have attained the age of 65 and require assistance with activities of daily living.

Expenses eligible for the tax credit include amounts paid for

  • medical care,
  • lodging away from home,
  • adult day services,
  • personal care,
  • respite care,
  • assistive technologies and devices (including remote health monitoring),
  • environmental modifications (including home modifications), and
  • counseling or training for a caregiver.

Strength in Diversity Act of 2026

This bill establishes a program through which the Department of Education must award planning and implementation grants to specified educational agencies (e.g., local educational agencies) to improve diversity and reduce or eliminate racial or socioeconomic isolation in publicly funded early childhood education programs, public elementary schools, or public secondary schools.

Strengthening Tools to Outlaw Poisonous Nitazenes Act or the STOP Nitazenes Act

This bill permanently places nitazenes as a class into schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act. Nitazenes are synthetic opioids similar to fentanyl that can be as potent or more potent than fentanyl. A schedule I controlled substance is a drug, substance, or chemical that has a high potential for abuse; has no currently accepted medical value; and is subject to regulatory controls and administrative, civil, and criminal penalties under the Controlled Substances Act.

", "updateDate": "2026-11-06T17:40:25Z", "versionCode": "00" }, { "actionDate": "2025-09-23", "actionDesc": "Introduced in House", "bill": { "congress": 119, "number": "5547", "originChamber": "House", "originChamberCode": "H", "title": "To amend the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 to provide for additional activities, resources, and data collection with respect to English learners, and for other purposes.", "type": "HR", "updateDateIncludingText": "2026-11-06", "url": "https://api.congress.gov/v3/bill/119/hr/5547?format=json" }, "currentChamber": "House", "currentChamberCode": "H", "lastSummaryUpdateDate": "2026-11-06T17:27:00Z", "text": "

This bill expands the allowable uses of grants under the English Language Acquisition program and expands related reporting requirements.

The English Language Acquisition program was designed to help ensure that English learners, including immigrant children and youth, attain English proficiency and develop high levels of academic achievement in English. Eligible entities receiving subgrants under the program are required to use funds for effective language instructional programs, professional development, and family and community engagement, and are authorized to use funds for additional related activities. Eligible entities include one or more local educational agencies (LEAs), or one or more LEAs partnering with a specified entity (e.g., an institution of higher education).

Under the bill, eligible entities may use subgrants for additional activities, such as (1) increasing the access of English learners and their parents to legal, educational, and financial resources and social services, including by providing such resources and services in the native language of such English learners and their parents; and (2) providing educators with culturally competent training and professional development.

The bill also requires eligible entities receiving subgrants to report additional information to their state educational agencies, such as providing information in the aggregate and disaggregate by English learners with a disability, ethnicity, race, and native language.

Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act

This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 a program that provides cybersecurity-related assistance and funding to rural electric cooperatives and municipal or small, investor-owned electric utilities. The bill also revises methods of awarding support and expands protections for information shared under the program.

This program, known as the Rural and Municipal Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program, is administered by the Department of Energy (DOE). Current law requires DOE to provide technical assistance and funding under the program on a competitive basis; under the bill, assistance and funding may be provided on a competitive or noncompetitive basis.

Current law also requires DOE to prioritize providing technical assistance and funding to certain entities, including entities that own defense critical electric infrastructure. The bill specifies that DOE must also prioritize entities that operate such infrastructure. (Defense critical electric infrastructure is electric infrastructure that (1) is located in the contiguous United States, and (2) serves a designated critical defense facility but is not owned or operated by the owner or operator of the critical facility.)

Finally, the bill expands an existing protection against disclosure to cover all information shared under the program by or with the federal government or a state, tribal, or local government. This provision protects against disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and other state, tribal, or local disclosure laws.

Volunteer Driver Tax Appreciation Act of 2025

This bill increases the standard mileage rate used in calculating the federal tax deduction for the use of a passenger automobile by an individual to transport persons (other than such individual) or property on behalf of a qualified charitable organization (e.g., certain veteran and fraternal groups, government entities, and religious organizations). The bill increases the rate from the standard charitable rate of 14 cents per mile to the standard business mileage rate, which is 70 cents per mile for 2025.
